sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Software vendors should sell maintenance of what users build
sections.para: Software in the way now feels offensive because I could rebuild the part I need; what stops me is maintenance. Vendors should become Wardley's villagers and town planners beneath users who explore on top. Firefox is the example: a good browser I could not bend, with about 73% of revenue from royalties.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Users will rebuild what they need; sell them maintenance
sections.para: Friction is now a choice because I could rebuild what I need, but I do not want to maintain it. The business is selling maintenance, letting users explore while the vendor keeps the core solid. Firefox is the example, the stock sell-off and Adobe clones are signs, and conversation beats settings.

sections.label: Every friction is now a decision
sections.line: Every software friction now prompts asking whether to rebuild
sections.para: Building custom interfaces for single moments means each obstacle prompts the question of whether to rebuild. A developer released open-source clones of seven Adobe applications this month. In February, after Claude Cowork plugins, Thomson Reuters fell about 18% in a day and RELX 14%. Rebuilding the 10% that matters is easy.

sections.label: What stops me is maintenance
sections.line: Maintenance, not building, is what users would pay for
sections.para: I could make my own Firefox, but I do not want to rebase it on every release or keep it working on laptop and iPad. That is a service I would pay the maker for: perhaps a pound a month, ten a year, fifty per change, five hundred for a company. It beats advertising or search deals.

sections.label: Become the villager and the town planner
sections.line: Vendors should be villagers and town planners under explorers
sections.para: Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners become a product strategy: users explore their own needs better than the company can, so the company should keep their builds working, turn popular ones into features and keep the core small. Ink & Switch's Malleable software comes closest, noting AI code generation alone does not remove the barriers.

sections.label: Firefox, as the example
sections.line: Firefox is a good browser I could not bend
sections.para: Compact mode was hidden from Firefox 89 until 157 on 29 September; the iPad still cannot hide the toolbar. Firefox lacks a serverless story agents need. Mozilla's 2024 revenue was $680 million, about 73% royalties, 86% of contract revenue from one customer, and browsing share is 2.8%. Firefox Enterprise sells the villager offer to institutions, not individuals.

sections.label: Settings are not the answer
sections.line: Engineering for variation beats piling up settings as debt
sections.para: Every setting is a code branch to test forever, and they accumulate into technical debt. Better is engineering: small primitives, clean extension points and design systems, as with five colour schemes on these sites instead of a dark mode feature. Serving millions of explorers needs a buildable core and a pipeline keeping personal versions working.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Products are not dead; the positioning is a proposal
sections.para: The Adobe clones are early and most users will rebuild nothing. No vendor was found selling maintenance to individuals, though Mozilla sells custom development to organisations. The prices are illustrative, some Firefox complaints were fixed in September but not the iPad one, and the sell-off had many causes.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: Wardley, Ink & Switch, Mozilla, Reuters, StatCounter
sections.para: Written by the site's agent from my voice memo of 16 October 2026. Sources include Simon Wardley on Explorer, Villager and Town Planners and ILC, Ink & Switch's Malleable software, Reuters on the February sell-off, the photocraft clones in Al Jazeera, Mozilla's Firefox Enterprise, release notes and 2024 accounts, StatCounter and firefox-lambda.
